author: Carlos Martinez
title: The Porsche 963 GTP on iRacing: Hybrid Power and a Different Kind of Patience
description: My honest impressions racing the Porsche 963 GTP on iRacing — setup notes, wheel feel, and who this car actually suits.

sections.p: I run all of this from a fixed-aluminium-extrusion cockpit with a ~MOZA R9 direct drive wheelbase and ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals — no motion, no fancy paint, just a rig built to be honest about what the car is doing. Here's what the Porsche 963 GTP has actually been like to race, across the tracks I run most — not a spec-sheet rundown, just what I've actually noticed after enough laps to trust my own impressions.

I try to give a car a genuinely fair chance before forming an opinion on it — a session or two of just getting comfortable before I start comparing it to anything else I race. The Porsche 963 GTP is a good example of a car that rewarded that patience; my first impression and my impression after a few weeks weren't quite the same.

sections.h2: What this car is really like to drive

sections.p: The hybrid deployment adds a layer of strategy I don't have to think about in a GT3 car — managing when power comes in changes how you plan a corner exit, not just how hard you can push.

That character shows up most clearly once you're pushing near the limit rather than cruising around at seven-tenths — which is honestly true of most race cars, but it's worth saying plainly here because a lot of first impressions of the Porsche 963 GTP get formed in that first cautious session and then never get revisited.

list: Getting comfortable with the hybrid system's deployment window took longer than learning the car's cornering limits
I run a more conservative aero setup than in a GT3 car since the 963's higher top speed makes drag a bigger factor over a full stint
Fuel and energy management became something I actively plan around rather than an afterthought, closer to real endurance racing than sprint GT3 racing

sections.p: As with any setup notes, I'd treat these as a starting direction rather than a fixed recipe — track-specific demands, personal preference, and even the specific series rules you're racing under can all shift what actually works best. Change one thing at a time and judge it against a stopwatch, not just a feeling.

sections.h2: How it feels through the wheel

sections.p: Through the ~MOZA R9, the 963's higher cornering speeds and downforce load come through as noticeably heavier steering than any GT3 car I run — the extra grip is obvious the moment you turn the wheel.

Pedal feel matters just as much here as wheel feel, and I'd say the same logic applies to the ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals I run — a car's braking character comes through in how the pedal resists your foot, not just in how the car decelerates on screen. Cars with different weight distributions like the Porsche 963 GTP genuinely reward paying attention to that resistance curve rather than just stomping to a fixed travel point every time.

sections.tip: Spend time specifically learning the hybrid deployment before worrying about outright pace — understanding when power is and isn't available changes how you approach every corner exit.

sections.h2: Common mistakes I see (and made myself) in this car

list: Carrying over setup habits from a different car class instead of respecting what the Porsche 963 GTP specifically rewards
Judging the car's limit too early, in the first session, before tires and the driver are both actually warmed up
Ignoring how the car's character changes over a longer run as tires wear, rather than just tuning for a single fast lap

sections.p: Endurance racing fans and anyone curious about prototype-class cars and hybrid systems, especially drivers who already enjoy the strategic side of tire and fuel management.

sections.h2: Practice plan for getting comfortable with this car

olist: Spend a full session with no other cars on track just learning where the Porsche 963 GTP's grip limit actually is in isolation
Run a handful of laps intentionally over the limit in a low-stakes session so you know what the car's warning signs feel like before you're relying on avoiding them under race pressure
Do at least one longer run at race pace rather than qualifying pace before your first real race in the car, so tire wear and fuel load aren't a surprise
Race it in a lower-pressure series first if you can, before bringing it into a series or split where the stakes and traffic density are higher

sections.p: That progression matters more with the Porsche 963 GTP than it might with a car you're already deeply familiar with, simply because every car has its own specific way of warning you before it lets go, and you can't actually learn that warning from reading about it — only from spending time right at the edge of it in a controlled setting.

sections.h2: What I'd change about my own approach next time

sections.p: Looking back at my early sessions in the Porsche 963 GTP, I spent too long trying to force a setup and driving style that worked well in a different car onto it, rather than treating it as its own thing with its own demands from lap one. That cost me more time than any actual mechanical shortcoming in the car itself, and it's a mistake I think a lot of drivers make whenever they change car class — old habits are comfortable, but comfortable isn't the same as correct for the car you're actually in.

If I were starting over with this car today, I'd spend the first full session purely on getting comfortable with its specific braking and rotation character before touching the setup at all — changing the car's balance before you actually understand its default behavior just muddies the feedback you're trying to learn from.

sections.h2: A quick note on iRating and Safety Rating in this car

sections.p: Jumping into a new car class, including the Porsche 963 GTP, resets some of your comfort even if your iRating and Safety Rating carry over. I'd expect a small dip in results for the first several races purely from unfamiliarity, and I wouldn't read too much into it — it's a normal, temporary cost of learning something new, not a sign you've actually gotten worse at racing in general.

If you're deciding what to race next, it's worth reading my notes on endurance racing and driver swaps too — car choice and track choice both matter more than people give them credit for when you're building consistency, and the two decisions usually aren't independent of each other.

faqs.q: Is the Porsche 963 GTP good for a driver moving up in car class?
faqs.a: Generally yes, provided the jump in grip and speed from your current car isn't too large — I'd recommend a session or two of just getting comfortable before pushing for outright pace.

faqs.q: What wheelbase do you race this car on?
faqs.a: I run a ~MOZA R9 with ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals for all my iRacing sessions, including this car.

faqs.q: Do the setup notes here apply across all tracks?
faqs.a: They're a starting point rather than a fixed answer — I adjust from this baseline depending on the specific track's demands.
That depends on your current experience level more than the car itself — see the 'who this car suits' section above for my honest take.
